item.title: Sandworm ClickFix Lures, TELEPUZ and ClickLock Stealers, Scattered Spider Sentences
item.content:encoded:
CISA orders feds to patch actively exploited Oracle flaw by Saturday — Must Read

CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch Oracle E-Business Suite systems by July 18 after confirming active exploitation of critical flaw CVE-2026-46817, which can let unauthenticated attackers take over Oracle Payments via HTTP. Oracle patched the issue in May, but exposed and unpatched EBS instances remain at risk.

  • CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite instances by Saturday, July 18, after adding CVE-2026-46817 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
  • CVE-2026-46817 affects the File Transmission component of Oracle Payments in Oracle E-Business Suite and allows unauthenticated attackers with HTTP network access to compromise Oracle Payments.
  • Oracle released security updates for CVE-2026-46817 in its May 2026 Critical Security Patch Update and urged customers to apply patches without delay.
  • Threat intelligence company Defused reported on June 29 that it observed exploitation of CVE-2026-46817 on Oracle E-Business honeypots despite no known public proof-of-concept code.
  • Shadowserver tracks more than 1,000 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, with more than half located in the United States.

Sandworm hackers have a CAPTCHA trick for Ukrainians — Must Read

Ukraine’s CERT says Russia-linked Sandworm hackers are using fake CAPTCHA prompts on compromised websites to trick Ukrainian targets into pasting PowerShell commands that install malware. The group is also continuing older social-engineering tactics, including bogus Android security apps, pirated software installers and fake antivirus files shared via Signal.

  • Ukraine's CERT-UA said Russian military intelligence hackers known as Sandworm have increasingly used fake CAPTCHA prompts on compromised websites to trick Ukrainian targets into infecting their own Windows computers.
  • The fake CAPTCHA prompts instruct users to copy and paste a PowerShell command that downloads malware, giving hackers access to the computer and the ability to deploy additional tools later.
  • CERT-UA observed the ClickFix technique on more than 10 compromised websites during June and July but did not report the number of compromised devices.
  • Researchers identified malware and tools called GhettoVibe, ScoutCurl, FluidLeech and LoadLoop in connection with the activity.
  • CERT-UA said Sandworm also continues to use older tactics, including fake Android security apps distributed through messaging apps, backdoored Windows and Office installers on torrent sites, and bogus antivirus files shared through Signal.

Russian hackers trojanize WebEx, Zoom apps to push Starland malware — Must Read

Russian threat actor UAT-11795 is distributing trojanized installers for apps like WebEx, Zoom, MobaXterm, DBeaver, and FaceIT to deploy the new Starland RAT, which steals credentials, crypto wallet data, and system information. Users should only download software from official sources and avoid running unfamiliar commands found online.

  • A financially motivated Russian threat actor tracked as UAT-11795 is using trojanized installers for legitimate software including MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, and FaceIT to deploy a new backdoor called Starland RAT.
  • Cisco Talos said the attacks have been occurring since at least June 2025 and have mainly targeted users in the United States, with victims also observed in Germany, Romania, and Venezuela.
  • The attack chain starts with an HTA file that retrieves a trojanized NSIS installer containing a Python loader disguised as LICENSE.txt, which establishes persistence and decrypts and loads Starland RAT.
  • Starland RAT can collect browser data, cryptocurrency wallet assets, system details, and Active Directory information, and it can also capture screenshots, execute shell commands, inject shellcode, and download additional payloads.
  • Cisco Talos reported that UAT-11795 also uses a previously undocumented PowerShell C2 framework called WLDR and a fallback command-and-control mechanism involving a Polygon smart contract with an XOR-encrypted fallback domain.

Daxin Resurfaces in Taiwan Alongside Stupig Pre-Login SYSTEM Backdoor — Should Read

Symantec found the China-linked Daxin rootkit active again on a Taiwan manufacturing host, alongside a newly reported Stupig backdoor that gives attackers SYSTEM-level command execution from the Windows logon screen before any user signs in. The discovery suggests a highly stealthy espionage operation may have persisted undetected for years.

  • Symantec and Carbon Black researchers found the Daxin kernel-mode rootkit running on a compromised host in Taiwan in 2026 after more than four years without public reporting of the malware.
  • The same host, belonging to a Taiwan-based subsidiary of a multinational high-tech manufacturer, was also infected with a previously unreported backdoor called Stupig.
  • Stupig persists by registering as a keyboard-layout provider, causing Windows to load it into winlogon.exe at startup and allowing commands entered with the username prefix “stupig” to run with SYSTEM privileges from the logon screen.
  • Daxin avoids conventional outbound command-and-control by monitoring incoming TCP traffic for specific patterns and hijacking existing legitimate connections for encrypted communications.
  • Broadcom said the compromised machine may have been exposed through an outdated Digiwin single sign-on portal that used end-of-life Java Development Kit 1.5 and 1.6 installations from 2009 to 2011.

New ClickLock macOS Stealer Kills Apps Every 210ms Until Victims Type Their Password — Should Read

ClickLock Stealer is a new macOS infostealer that coerces victims into entering their login password by repeatedly killing key apps until they comply. Once entered, it steals Keychain data, Chrome encryption keys, browser credentials, cookies, crypto wallets, and other sensitive files, with persistence and a reverse shell potentially left behind.

  • ClickLock Stealer is a new macOS infostealer that arrives as a command pasted into Terminal and uses a fake system dialog to request the victim’s login password.
  • If the victim cancels the initial password prompt, ClickLock installs LaunchAgents that repeatedly kill Finder, Dock, Spotlight, Terminal, Activity Monitor, and major browsers every 210 milliseconds at the next login until a password is entered.
  • Group-IB observed at least 100 ClickLock targets across 33 countries since May, with more than half of the targets in Europe.
  • After a successful run, ClickLock can exfiltrate the validated macOS login password, Chrome’s Safe Storage AES key, browser credentials and cookies, crypto wallet data, password manager vaults, the Keychain, shell history, and FileZilla saved server credentials.
  • Group-IB reported that the backdoor component named goyim is largely copied from the public GSocket deploy script and uses a relay at gsnc[.]eu:67, while the stolen data is sent through Telegram bots.

GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and exfiltration — Should Read

Kaspersky reports that GoSerpent, a Go-based RAT targeting government and diplomatic entities in Southeast Asia, has evolved into a coordinated toolset for long-term espionage. The attackers use GoSerpent, Stowaway, ThumbcacheService, credential dumpers, and TmcLoader/TmcPayload together to collect sensitive files, steal credentials, and later exfiltrate the data through network shares.

  • Kaspersky discovered malicious activity in February 2026 that had been ongoing since late 2025 and targeted government and diplomatic entities in Southeast Asia.
  • The main malware, GoSerpent, is a Go-based remote access Trojan with proxy capabilities that receives encrypted command-line arguments and communicates with command-and-control servers using ChaCha20 encryption.
  • The attackers used GoSerpent to deploy ThumbcacheService to collect sensitive files and credential dumping tools including Mimikatz and QuarksDumpLocalHash.
  • In May 2026, the threat actor returned with Stowaway and a two-stage exfiltration tool called TmcLoader/TmcPayload to move previously collected data through network shares.
  • The article states that GoSerpent has been used since at least 2021 and that there are indications of a possible link to the TetrisPhantom threat actor, though attribution remains uncertain.

20+ Hijacked Government Websites Became an Attack Channel — Should Read

ANY.RUN researchers found that the PhantomEnigma campaign hijacked more than 20 Brazilian government websites and compromised email accounts to deliver malware through trusted-looking police and government lures. The operation uses a modular Node.js/Electron backdoor that can persist, execute commands, and deploy additional payloads, raising risk for banks and public agencies.

  • ANY.RUN researchers uncovered an active PhantomEnigma campaign that hijacked more than 20 Brazilian government websites and used them as malware delivery channels.
  • The campaign used fake police-themed or official-document lures, compromised mailboxes that passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks, and redirects through compromised .gov.br hosts or police-themed lookalike domains.
  • The observed infection chain included a malicious installer, a patched Electron application, activation of a Node.js backdoor, rotating command-and-control infrastructure, and delivery of additional payloads such as stealers, loaders, remote management software, and other malware.
  • The PhantomEnigma backdoor collected system and user details, created a persistent machine ID, established persistence, checked for commands every 180 seconds, executed JavaScript through eval(), and downloaded executable payloads.
  • The article states that the campaign creates risks for banks and public-sector organizations, including credential compromise, unauthorized access, fraud, data exposure, and operational disruption.

New TELEPUZ Malware Spreads via ClickFix to Steal Data and Run Commands — Should Read

A new modular malware called TELEPUZ is spreading through ClickFix lures that trick users into running malicious PowerShell commands, enabling data theft, command execution, persistence, and browser cookie theft. Researchers say its active development and daily builds suggest an emerging malware-as-a-service operation.

  • Elastic Security Labs reported that a new modular malware called TELEPUZ has been spreading through websites infected with ClickFix lures since late April 2026.
  • The TELEPUZ infection chain uses PowerShell to download a second-stage payload, a Go variant of Vidar Stealer, which harvests sensitive data and deploys a stager that launches telepuz.dll with rundll32.exe.
  • TELEPUZ uses obfuscation, anti-virtual-machine checks, geolocation checks, sandbox identifier checks, NTDLL unhooking, AMSI and ETW disabling, debugger detection, and validation of its parent process before continuing execution.
  • After identifying a victim session, TELEPUZ can elevate privileges, attempt to gain SYSTEM privileges by stealing a token from selected Windows processes, and register itself as a service loaded through a new svchost.exe instance.
  • TELEPUZ communicates with its command-and-control server over WebSockets and can perform file operations, keystroke logging, command execution, process management, screenshot capture, web injection, Chromium cookie extraction, and downloading and running executables and DLL modules.

New Agent Data Injection Attack Can Make AI Agents Misclick or Run Attacker Commands — Should Read

Researchers described a new “agent data injection” technique that can trick AI agents by corrupting trusted-looking data fields, causing actions like misclicks, command execution, or unsafe code merges without using obvious malicious instructions. Existing prompt-injection defenses often miss it, while randomized element or field identifiers and stronger data provenance controls appear more effective.

  • Researchers from Seoul National University, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and Largosoft described a new class of attack called agent data injection, where attacker-controlled input is presented as trusted data rather than as an explicit malicious instruction.
  • The researchers built working attacks against web agents including Claude in Chrome, Google Antigravity, and Nanobrowser, as well as coding assistants including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Google Gemini CLI.
  • In the demonstrated web-agent attack, a planted product review reused the ID of a real button so an agent intending to click “Read More” could instead click “Buy Now.”
  • In the demonstrated coding-assistant attacks, a GitHub comment could forge a maintainer author line to get an agent to run an attacker’s command, and a malicious pull request could fake a clean check result to influence an agent’s review.
  • The article says purpose-built agent defenses blocked classic instruction-smuggling attacks almost entirely in tests, but agent data injection still succeeded up to 50% of the time.

23andMe to pay $18 million in new genetics data breach settlement — Should Read

23andMe will pay $18 million to settle claims by 43 attorneys general that weak security allowed a 2023 credential-stuffing breach exposing genetic ancestry data from 6.9 million customers. The settlement also imposes stricter security requirements and preserves consumers’ rights to delete their data.

  • 23andMe, now Chrome Holding Co., agreed to pay $18 million to settle claims from 43 attorneys general that it failed to protect customers' genetic data.
  • The company disclosed in October 2023 that credential-stuffing attacks went unnoticed from April 2023 to September 2023 and led to the theft of data belonging to 6.9 million customers.
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James said investigators found that 23andMe lacked basic safeguards such as password blocklisting, multifactor authentication, adequate rate limiting, intrusion prevention, and breach-detection monitoring.
  • The settlement requires new security measures at TTAM, including a data security advisory board, risk analysis protocols, and continued consumer rights to delete their data.
  • The 2023 breach also led to class-action lawsuits, a $30 million class action settlement, Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings, and a £2.31 million fine from the UK Information Commissioner's Office.

Scattered Spider hackers sentenced to 5.5 years over £29 million Transport for London hack — Should Read

Two leading Scattered Spider members were sentenced to 5.5 years in prison for the 2024 Transport for London hack, which disrupted critical systems, exposed customer data, and cost £29 million to recover. UK authorities said the case significantly disrupted one of the country’s most serious cybercrime threats.

  • Thalha Jubair and Owen Flowers were each sentenced to five years and six months in prison after pleading guilty to offenses under Section 3ZA of the Computer Misuse Act for the 2024 Transport for London cyberattack.
  • The attack disrupted Transport for London operations, made 148 internal systems unavailable, forced 27,000 employees to complete in-person password resets, exposed customer data, and cost £29 million in recovery expenses.
  • The breach affected Transport for London’s Oyster refund system, delaying some passenger refunds, and temporarily suspended applications for Oyster photocards used by children and young people.
  • The National Crime Agency identified Jubair and Flowers as leading members of Scattered Spider, an English-speaking cybercriminal network linked to attacks on airlines, retailers, insurers, and technology companies in the U.K. and United States.
  • British authorities said the case was the largest cybercrime prosecution ever brought before a U.K. court and only the second prosecution under the U.K.’s most serious Computer Misuse Act offense.

A Trusted Domain, a Voicemail, and a Windows .EXE — Should Read

A phishing email sent from a legitimately authenticated nonprofit domain used a voicemail lure to deliver a malicious Windows executable from a newly registered domain. The key takeaway is that SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and sender reputation do not prove an email is safe when a real account or trusted domain is abused.

  • A phishing email posing as a voicemail notification was sent from a legitimate nonprofit domain and passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication.
  • Six of the seven links in the message pointed to the real nonprofit organization’s website or social pages and were clean.
  • The link labeled “Mailbox” downloaded a Windows executable named hmlineea.exe from db2000.net, a domain registered 26 days before delivery with privacy-protected registration.
  • Public sandbox analysis of hmlineea.exe returned malicious behavior, and automated link analysis scored the URL at 0.95 on a 0-to-1 risk scale.
  • IRONSCALES Themis flagged the message based on behavior, including a first-time external sender, a malicious payload host, and language and structure matching prior phishing patterns.

Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro reach end of support in 90 days — Should Read

Microsoft says Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro, along with Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016, will stop receiving security and preview updates on October 13, 2026. Users should upgrade to Windows 11 25H2 to remain protected.

  • Microsoft announced that Windows 11 version 24H2 Home and Pro editions and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 will reach end of updates on October 13, 2026.
  • After October 13, 2026, devices running those editions will no longer receive monthly security and non-security preview updates containing protections from the latest security threats.
  • Windows 11 version 24H2 Enterprise and Education editions will remain under mainstream support until October 12, 2027.
  • Microsoft advises customers to upgrade to Windows 11 version 25H2, also known as the Windows 11 2025 Update.
  • Devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro that are not managed by IT departments will receive the Windows 11 25H2 update automatically, but users can postpone the update or choose when to restart.

Benchmarking 13 AI models on rediscovering known CVEs — May Read

A benchmark of 13 AI models found GPT-5.6 had the best CVE rediscovery recall, but repeated runs of cheaper mid-tier models often matched or beat a single flagship run at much lower cost. The biggest remaining challenge is finding vulnerabilities that require deeper reasoning across complex code paths rather than obvious dangerous sinks.

  • The benchmark tested 13 AI models against 26 known vulnerabilities from the GitHub advisory database using an AI Code Analysis harness built for code auditing.
  • GPT-5.6 achieved the highest recall score, rediscovering 23 of 26 CVEs, while grok-4.5 found 20 and the Claude Opus models found between 15 and 18.
  • Every model rediscovered both critical CVEs, and the largest performance differences appeared on high- and medium-severity findings.
  • Pooling three runs of the same model improved results because different runs found different subsets of bugs, with gpt-5.4-nano rising from no more than 14 in a single run to 18 of 26 across three runs.
  • The article concludes that running cheaper models multiple times can find more vulnerabilities for less money than a single pass of a more expensive flagship model.

AI Can Find Bugs, But Human Knowledge Still Proves Them — Optional

AI can speed up offensive security testing by generating leads, payloads, and reports, but it cannot replace human validation. Security teams should treat AI output as hypotheses until a skilled tester proves reachability, exploitability, impact, and the fix.

  • AI-assisted tools can quickly read code, generate payloads, summarize attack surfaces, explain unfamiliar APIs, and run repetitive testing workflows, but their output is not evidence that a vulnerability exists in a deployed environment.
  • Bug bounty programs and maintainers are already seeing more low-quality AI-generated reports with polished language but thin evidence, creating unnecessary triage burden.
  • The article argues that testers must prove reachability, attacker control, boundary crossing, reproducible steps, demonstrated impact, and relevance in the deployed configuration before promoting a lead to a finding.
  • Experienced offensive security practitioners remain valuable because they understand systems well enough to interpret tool output, adapt when first attempts fail, and avoid overstating severity.
  • The article says AI should be used to generate leads, suggest tests, and reduce repetitive work, while skilled humans retain responsibility for validation and final judgment.

The Hunter's Paradox: Is it time to embrace automated threat hunting? — Optional

The author argues that threat hunting should shift from being strictly human-driven to reasoning-driven, allowing AI to execute narrowly scoped hunts because humans can no longer keep pace with security data volume and speed. But AI must be constrained with tight focus, strict access controls, graduated autonomy, and human ownership of strategy and novel hunting ideas.

  • The author describes the “Hunter’s Paradox” as the need to use AI for threat hunting because humans cannot keep up with security data volume and speed, while also recognizing that AI cannot be fully trusted.
  • The article says AI struggles with deception because attackers routinely create misleading data and AI systems tend to take the information they receive at face value.
  • The author proposes redefining threat hunting from a “manual or machine-assisted” process to a “reasoning-driven” process for finding security incidents missed by automated detection systems.
  • The article recommends limiting AI-driven hunting with tight focus, strict access controls and rules, and gradual increases in autonomy rather than giving AI broad independence.
  • The author argues that humans should remain responsible for deciding what is worth hunting for and for creating novel analysis approaches, while AI executes hunts within those human-defined boundaries.

The best defenders build AI agents together: Join Tenable for Swarm at Black Hat ’26 — Optional

Tenable is hosting Swarm at Black Hat USA 2026, a hands-on event for security practitioners to collaboratively build open-source agentic AI tools, skills, and MCP servers. The goal is to move AI security automation out of isolated efforts and into shared tooling for collective defense.

  • Tenable is hosting Swarm, a hands-on agentic AI build event at Black Hat USA 2026 sponsored by AWS and presented with support from Anthropic.
  • The event is intended for security practitioners to collaborate on open-source AI security agents, MCP servers, skills, and playbooks for workflows such as triage, remediation, orchestration, and executive reporting.
  • The article says security teams are already building agentic AI tools to reduce manual work in areas such as phishing email triage, proactive threat hunting, alert triage, detection writing, and security automation.
  • Tenable argues that many practitioners currently build agentic AI tools in isolation, causing teams to duplicate work and miss the benefits of shared results.
  • The article cites Gartner as saying that by 2028 an average global Fortune 500 enterprise will have more than 150,000 AI agents in use, up from fewer than 15 in 2025.
